title: Nigeria’s Big Bet on Health Care
content: Nigeria’s dependence on imported medicines and medical equipment leaves families exposed to exchange-rate fluctuations and hospitals at the mercy of global supply chains. Expanding domestic manufacturing is essential to reducing the cost of treatment and ensuring that more Nigerians can access quality care.

title: What Should the Nvidia Board Do?
content: The proper role of any corporate board is to strike a careful balance between stakeholders. In Nvidia's case, the board will have to consider not just the current trading price, but also how its decisions will affect the landscape in which it operates, its employees, and its license to trade.

title: The Roots of Macron’s Failure
content: Although French President Emmanuel Macron has certainly made mistakes, his troubled presidency is symptomatic of a deeper problem. In the end, he failed to build something truly enduring because he was seduced by the same monarchical impulse that is a recurring feature of French political culture.

title: Yalta in Shenzhen?
content: In principle, the planned summit of the US, Russian, and Chinese presidents could usefully address what should be done to limit the proliferation of nuclear weapons, ensure that AI is more a force for good than harm, and end ongoing wars and prevent new ones. But principle is one thing; in practice, we are likely to see something else.

title: The Perverse Effects of the AI Investment Boom
content: As big tech companies increasingly turn to debt markets to finance massive investments in AI data centers, they are competing for the same pools of capital as many governments. With interest rates already high and public demands for spending on the rise, the timing could hardly be worse for vulnerable economies.

content: The Democrats came out on top in the midterms by staying on message and focusing on affordability. But from voters’ perspective, there is an enormous difference between repudiating the administration and embracing the alternative.

title: Can Brexit Be Reversed?
content: British Prime Minister Andy Burnham has called Brexit a mistake, and opinion polls show that his proposal to "go all the way" and rejoin the European Union has majority support. But Brexit was won by a movement, and only a movement can reverse it.

content: Rather than assuming that traditional asset-allocation guidelines apply to current conditions, investors should position themselves for more volatility and uncertainty. The AI revolution and various structural forces mean that there is no going back to the familiar old diversification formula.

title: The Global Economy After the Iran War Ends
content: Even if the Iran war ended tomorrow, the global economy would not simply pick up where it left off. Reopening the Strait of Hormuz could bring down commodity prices and ease inflation, but postwar reconstruction could redirect capital away from the United States, undermining the AI supercycle and fueling de-dollarization.

title: Breaking Billionaires’ Political Grip
content: The US midterm elections showed that despite the outsize role of money in politics, even the biggest donors don’t always get their way. But defeating billionaires at the ballot box won’t stop them from buying political influence as long as the rules permit them to do so.

title: The Rare-Earth Game
content: China will probably not impose a rare-earth embargo, but it will keep the specter of one alive. And the West will probably not achieve self-sufficiency in this critical sector, but it will keep seeking to reduce its vulnerability to a supply shock through expensive capacity duplication and stockpiles.

title: Why Research Matters
content: Over the past 21 months, in the country that has leveraged research to greatest effect, the government is slashing funding for it, closing centers where it is done, politicizing grant-making decisions, and bullying its single biggest engine: universities. The costs will be far greater than many realize.

title: Africa Needs a Different Kind of Climate Finance
content: Roughly half of the climate finance that flows to Africa comes in the form of debt, with multilateral and bilateral development-finance institutions often lending at commercial rates to economies already struggling to carry the added costs. To maximize fiscal space, the instruments used to deliver climate finance need to change.

title: Effective Climate Action Requires Capable States
content: With delegations from around the world gathering for another international climate conference, the question today is not whether governments should do more to address the climate crisis, but whether they even have the capabilities to do so. After 40 years of free-market orthodoxy, many simply do not.

title: Why Is Mexico Defying Latin America’s Right Turn?
content: How Mexico’s left has managed to retain strong support is a key question of contemporary Latin American politics. The most likely answer centers on the ruling Morena party’s pragmatic brand of left-wing politics, which combines bold redistributive policies, greater security, and a willingness to compromise in the name of both.

content: The rush to develop central bank digital currencies has slowed as underwhelming demand and mounting costs have given governments second thoughts. But while the Federal Reserve and other central banks have shelved their plans, the European Central Bank is pressing ahead with its digital euro.

title: Medical AI Needs Bedside Manners
content: Even the most accurate medical AI tools have little value if they make patients uneasy or doctors find them too cumbersome. A comfort-by-design approach could overcome these obstacles by involving patients and practitioners in development and ensuring that new systems work with existing medical practices.

title: Oceania’s Three Goals for COP31
content: To make COP31 the “Blue COP,” delegates must recommit to keeping the 1.5° Celsius warming goal alive, reform the climate-finance system, and address our dependence on the fossil fuels driving the ocean's warming and acidification. Pacific countries have long championed these causes, but now the rest of the world must join them.

title: The Dance of Empires
content: Empires have a habit of preparing to fight the last war while their rivals work out how to win the next one. The US is no different, pouring its resources into military adventures while China slowly but steadily reclaims the scientific and technological leadership that once made it the world's greatest power.
